newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar lawyer savages chief witness.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar lawyer savages chief witness.

text.p: The lawyer for former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, on trial for rigging soccer matches, on Wednesday accused the chief witness of being a lying, vindictive no-hoper desperate to make money.
Lawyer Rodney Klevan said Chris Vincent had concocted a tissue of lies to bring down Grobbelaar after the keeper pulled out of a safari company the two men were running in Zimbabwe.

The prosecution's case rests largely on Vincent's claim that Grobbelaar confessed to rigging matches for a Far Eastern betting syndicate and tapes Vincent covertly recorded of talks with the keeper in which Grobbelaar seems to admit match-fixing.
The case is the first of its kind in England for more than 30 years and has sparked massive media interest.
Klevan painstakingly took Vincent through his testimony, often interrupting to accuse the balding Zimbabwean-born businessman of inventing the whole tale.
"You're lying about this and lying about anything you say about Grobbelaar and match-fixing," he snapped at one point.

The prosecution says Grobbelaar tried to fix at least four matches and was paid by Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim and former striker John Fashanu, both accused of being middlemen for the Far Eastern betting syndicate.
Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers is accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches. All four have pleaded not guilty.

Vincent said he had accompanied Grobbelaar on a trip to London in late November 1993 to pick up 40,000 pounds ($66,280) from Fashanu as a reward from the syndicate for throwing a match against Newcastle.
"What you're saying is absolute nonsense and is the figment of a very fertile imagination -- yours," said Klevan.
On Tuesday Vincent admitted he wanted to make as much money as he could from the case while crushing Grobbelaar, who he blames for the collapse of the safari company in July 1994.
Vincent invested none of his own money in the company, while Grobbelaar put in 65,000 pounds.
"In a flash the friendship had turned to hatred?" asked Klevan. "Yes, sir," replied Vincent.
"'Woe betide anyone who seems to cross Chris Vincent' -- isn't that a good epigraph for you?" asked Klevan.

"Reasonable, yes," replied Vincent, who admitted that from 1984 he had been the director of four failed companies in southern Africa and Britain, had not tried to repay creditors and had not told Grobbelaar about the bankruptcies.
Under close questioning, Vincent acknowledged his father had cut off contacts because he thought of him as a rogue and said he had not talked with his brother since the safari company collapsed.

"Your nearest and dearest don't want anything to do with you and your best mate you've treated worse than dirt," said Klevan. "As one person after another realised what you were like, they didn't want anything to do with you."
Vincent, awaiting trial for perverting the course of justice, remained calm during the morning session.
"What kind of man are you, Mr Vincent?" asked Klevan.
"Normal, sir," he replied.
"Then heaven help us from the abnormal, Mr Vincent," snapped the rotund lawyer.

The story broke when Vincent sold his story to the Sun newspaper, which helped him record the conversations with Grobbelaar. But Vincent said he was now in dispute with the paper, which he said had broken an agreement to pay him.
"So even the Sun newspaper can be added to the catalogue of people you've fallen out with?" Klevan asked. ($1=.6035 Pound)
